content: Colorado tick fever (CTF), also known as Mountain tick fever, Mountain fever, or American mountain fever, is an acute viral infection transmitted through the bite of an infected Rocky Mountain wood tick (Dermacentor andersoni). The causative agent, Colorado tick fever virus (CTFV), belongs to the genus Coltivirus. This virus primarily infects hematopoietic cells, particularly erythrocytes (red blood cells), which explains its transmission pathway within blood-sucking ticks and its potential for transmission through blood transfusion. The disease is predominantly found in the western United States and Canada, especially in high-altitude regions such as Colorado and Idaho. CTFV was first isolated from human blood in 1944. The virus particle is approximately 80 nm in diameter, non-enveloped, and contains a double-stranded RNA genome that is about 20,000 base pairs long, divided into 12 segments (Seg-1 to Seg-12). Viral replication in infected cells is associated with characteristic cytoplasmic granular matrices. Evidence suggests that the presence of the virus in mature erythrocytes results from its replication in hematopoietic erythrocyte precursor cells, followed by the maturation of these infected immature cells, rather than direct infection and replication in mature erythrocytes. Historically, Colorado tick fever remains a rare disease with limited historical documentation. There is no established classification system for this condition. Pathophysiologically, CTF is an Orbivirus or Coltivirus that chronically infects Rocky Mountain wood ticks. The virus typically targets bone marrow cells, disrupting the development of certain blood cells. Transmission occurs through the bite of an infected tick. Differentiating Colorado tick fever from other diseases is critical, as its clinical manifestations—fever, chills, headaches, body aches, and rash—closely resemble those of other tick-borne illnesses, particularly those caused by the Rickettsiae family. Misdiagnoses may include typhus-spotted fevers and ehrlichiosis. Epidemiologically, Colorado tick fever is rare, with only 83 cases reported between 2002 and 2012. The disease is primarily confined to the Rocky Mountain states, with occasional cases reported elsewhere in the United States. Its incidence appears to be independent of demographic factors or age. The primary risk factors for CTF include exposure to endemic environments and the timing of such exposure. The Rocky Mountain wood tick is the primary vector, and being bitten in an endemic area increases the risk of contracting the disease. The natural history of the disease involves an incubation period of 3–6 days after the tick bite, though it can extend up to 20 days. Patients typically experience a biphasic fever and illness, with symptoms lasting three days, subsiding, and then recurring for another 1–3 days. The virus can persist in the bloodstream for up to 120 days, necessitating precautions to prevent transmission through blood donation. Initial symptoms include fever, chills, headaches, retro-orbital pain, photophobia, muscle pain, generalized malaise, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and a flat or pimply rash. During the second phase, a high fever may return with worsening symptoms. Severe cases, particularly in children, may require hospitalization. Rare complications include aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and hemorrhagic fever. Clinically, Colorado tick fever presents with a range of symptoms, most commonly fever, chills, headache, body aches, and lethargy. Physical examination findings in the early stages include fever, lethargy, and generalized weakness. As the infection progresses, additional signs such as tachycardia, changes in blood pressure, sensitivity of the eyes and skin, and the appearance of a rash may develop. A biphasic fever is a hallmark feature of CTF, distinguishing it from other tick-borne illnesses. Laboratory confirmation of CTF involves a combination of tests. Immunofluorescence assay is the gold standard for detecting infection. Other diagnostic methods include complement fixation to viral components and acute and convalescent serology. Currently, there is no specific treatment for Colorado tick fever. Supportive care remains the primary approach, with hospitalization required in severe cases. Prevention strategies focus on avoiding tick bites in endemic areas. This can be achieved by limiting exposure to such regions or implementing protective measures when avoidance is impractical. Proper tick removal techniques are also essential to reduce the risk of infection.
